entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Ottoman dynasty (c.1299–1922) ruled one of history's longest-lived empires, spanning over six centuries, three continents, and the transition from medieval to modern era. At its height under Suleiman the Magnificent (r.1520-1566), the Ottoman Empire controlled Southeast Europe, western Asia, the Caucasus, North Africa, and the Arabian peninsula, encompassing roughly 15 million square kilometers.

Founded by Osman I in Anatolia from a small Turkic principality, the Ottomans conquered Constantinople in 1453 under Mehmed II — ending the Byzantine Empire and controlling the gateway between Europe and Asia. The 1453 conquest prompted European nations to seek sea routes to Asia, indirectly causing the Age of Exploration and Columbus's 1492 voyage. Ottoman administrative, legal, and architectural innovations — including the millet system allowing religious minorities autonomy — created a sophisticated multicultural governance model.

The 19th-century decline of the Ottoman 'sick man of Europe' — losing territories through nationalist movements and European wars — culminated in WWI defeat. The empire's dissolution created the modern Middle East's borders (largely through the Sykes-Picot Agreement), the Turkish Republic under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, and the Palestinian mandate whose tensions persist today. Six centuries of Ottoman rule shaped the cultures of 30+ modern nations.
